title: Name That Drift
blurb: Eight ways a model goes stale. Sort each production symptom into the one it actually is.
source: Gama et al. (2014), A survey on concept drift adaptation · Moreno-Torres et al. (2012), A unifying view on dataset shift · NIST AI RMF 1.0 MEASURE 2.4
hint: Drag each production symptom onto the kind of drift it describes. The question is always which distribution moved — the inputs, the labels, the outputs, or the relationship between them.
note: An upstream data break gets a zone of its own because it looks identical to real drift on every dashboard, and the correct response is the opposite one: fix the feed, never retrain on it.

zones.name: Covariate drift
zones.def: P(X) moves. The inputs look different, but the rule mapping inputs to outcomes still holds.

zones.name: Concept drift — sudden
zones.def: P(Y|X) changes abruptly at a point in time. The old rule stops applying overnight.

zones.name: Concept drift — gradual
zones.def: The old and new rules coexist, with the new one appearing in an increasing share of cases.

zones.name: Concept drift — incremental
zones.def: The rule itself moves continuously through intermediate states rather than switching between two.

zones.name: Concept drift — recurring
zones.def: A previously seen rule returns on a cycle. Seasonality is the common case.

zones.name: Label shift
zones.def: P(Y) moves — the mix of outcomes changes — while the features given the outcome behave as before.

zones.name: Prediction drift
zones.def: The model's output distribution moves. It is a symptom, observable without any labels, not a diagnosis.

zones.name: Upstream data break
zones.def: Nothing in the world changed. A pipeline, schema, unit or default changed, and the model is being fed corrupted input.

items.label: A loan model was trained on applicants aged 25–60. After a marketing push into a student market, a third of applications now come from under-25s. Repayment behaviour for any given profile is unchanged.
items.why: The input mix moved into a region the training data barely covered, but the relationship between profile and repayment is intact. That is P(X) moving with P(Y|X) held — covariate drift, and the fix is coverage, not a new rule.

items.label: A speech model trained mostly on studio recordings now receives a large share of calls from mobile handsets in noisy streets. Words still mean what they meant.
items.why: Acoustic conditions are an input property. The mapping from audio to text has not changed; the model is simply operating outside the input region it learned well.

items.label: A demand model built on one country's stores is rolled out to three more countries. The products, the seasons and the buying logic are the same; the store profiles are not.
items.why: This is the textbook case of the training distribution not covering the deployment distribution. Nothing about how demand is generated changed — only which inputs are being seen.

items.label: A fraud model's precision collapses in a single week. Investigators find a new attack technique that began on a specific date and is now the dominant pattern.
items.why: The same feature values that meant legitimate last month now mean fraud. P(Y|X) changed, and it changed at a point in time — an abrupt concept change, not a shift in who is transacting.

items.label: A pricing model degrades overnight when a regulator caps a fee that the model had learned to treat as a strong signal of customer segment.
items.why: A rule change external to the data instantaneously rewires what the feature means. Retraining on post-change data is the fix; nothing about the pre-change data is recoverable.

items.label: A content classifier is fine until a platform policy change takes effect on the first of the month, after which its 'acceptable' label no longer matches moderator decisions.
items.why: The target definition itself was redefined on a date. The features are unchanged; the ground truth moved under them.

items.label: Over eight months, a churn model's accuracy slides as a competitor's new plan is adopted by more and more customers. Both the old and the new churn dynamics are visible in the data throughout.
items.why: Two regimes coexist, with the newer one taking an increasing share of cases. That mixture over time is the signature of gradual drift, and it is why a single change point cannot be found.

items.label: A recommendation model degrades slowly as an older cohort of users is progressively replaced by a younger one with different tastes. For a long period both behaviours are present.
items.why: Two populations with two different input-to-outcome rules overlap during the transition. Detection is late precisely because no single week looks anomalous.

items.label: A spam filter weakens over a year as senders migrate from one template family to another, with a long period where both templates arrive in quantity.
items.why: Old and new concepts are both live during the switchover. Compare it with incremental drift, where there are no two regimes, just one that keeps moving.

items.label: A delivery-time model's error grows steadily month after month as traffic congestion worsens a little at a time. There is no point at which behaviour jumps and no earlier regime to return to.
items.why: The relationship is passing continuously through intermediate states rather than alternating between two defined regimes. Rolling-window retraining suits this; change-point detection will find nothing.

items.label: A sensor-based quality model drifts as a machine's components wear, degrading a fraction of a percent per week with no discontinuity.
items.why: Physical wear moves the input-to-outcome mapping smoothly and monotonically. Each week is a slightly new concept, not a mixture of an old and a new one.

items.label: A language model's topical accuracy erodes month by month as vocabulary and usage evolve, with no single event responsible.
items.why: Continuous, directional movement of the concept with no change point and no return. The remedy is a refresh cadence, not an alarm threshold.

items.label: A retail forecasting model fails every December, recovers in January, and fails again the following December.
items.why: A previously seen concept returns on a cycle. The right response is to model the seasonality or keep the seasonal model, not to retrain in a panic each winter.

items.label: An energy demand model's errors follow a weekday/weekend pattern that repeats indefinitely.
items.why: The alternating regimes are both known and both come back. Retraining on the most recent window alone would make the model permanently wrong for whichever regime it last saw.

items.label: A staffing model degrades during each school holiday and returns to normal afterwards, year after year.
items.why: Recurring context. Keeping and reselecting historical models per context beats discarding them, because the old concept is guaranteed to return.

items.label: A disease screening model's positive rate falls sharply after a successful vaccination campaign. Symptoms still indicate the disease exactly as before.
items.why: The prevalence of the outcome fell — P(Y) moved — while P(X|Y) held. Thresholds and any prior-dependent calibration need adjusting; the learned relationship does not.

items.label: A fraud model trained when 3% of transactions were fraudulent now operates where 0.5% are, because of controls introduced elsewhere. Fraudulent transactions look the same as ever.
items.why: The base rate changed, so every probability the model emits is miscalibrated even though its discrimination is unaffected. Prior correction fixes this without retraining.

items.label: A defect classifier is moved from a pilot line with a 20% defect rate to a mature line with 2%. Defects present identically on both.
items.why: Only the class prior changed. Reading this as covariate drift leads to pointless feature work; reading it as label shift leads to a threshold recalibration that actually works.

items.label: Monitoring shows the share of 'approve' decisions rising from 61% to 78% over six weeks. No labels have arrived yet, so quality cannot be measured.
items.why: The output distribution moved. That is an alert, not a diagnosis: it can be caused by covariate drift, label shift, a broken feed, or a genuinely changed population. It is what you watch when labels are delayed.

items.label: A model's average predicted probability climbs steadily while the input feature distributions look stable on every chart.
items.why: Outputs moving without visible input movement usually means the movement is in a feature interaction or a feature nobody is monitoring. The finding is real; the cause is still unidentified.

items.label: After a model version is deployed, the distribution of scores shifts noticeably even though the incoming data is identical to last week's.
items.why: Same inputs, different outputs means the change is in the model, not the world. Version-to-version prediction drift is the reason a new release is compared on a fixed reference sample.

items.label: A revenue feature's mean drops to a third of its usual value overnight. An upstream team switched the field from cents to whole units the same night.
items.why: The world did not change; the unit did. Retraining here would teach the model to treat corrupted values as normal and make the eventual fix look like a new regression.

items.label: A categorical feature suddenly shows 40% nulls. A schema change renamed the source column and the join now misses.
items.why: A pipeline defect presents exactly like sudden drift on a drift dashboard. The tell is that the change coincides with a deploy or schema event rather than anything in the world.

items.label: A model's inputs shift the moment a vendor changes an API default, silently replacing missing values with zero instead of omitting them.
items.why: Zeros that mean 'missing' are read by the model as a real, extreme value. The fix is upstream contract enforcement and null semantics, never a retrain.
